claims.claim: Primary energy is energy from natural sources (fossil fuels, nuclear fuel, renewables) before conversion; electricity is a secondary energy carrier produced from primary sources.
In 2025, U.S. primary energy consumption was about 96 quads: petroleum 35.9 (37%), natural gas 34.6 (36%), coal 8.7 (9%), renewables 8.8 (9%), nuclear 8.2 (9%); fossil fuels supplied about 82%.

Counting direct primary energy use, in 2025 U.S. end-use sectors were transportation 28.2 quads (37%), industrial 26.6 (35%), residential 11.8 (15%), commercial 9.9 (13%); building sectors' shares rise when electricity and its losses are distributed to them.
Power (watt) is the rate of energy use; energy (watt-hour, joule) is power times time. 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ ≈ 3,412 BTU; 1 quad = 10^15 BTU; 1 BTU ≈ 1,055 J.

U.S. energy intensity (energy per real dollar of GDP) has declined for decades; EIA's AEO2020 projected energy use growing ~0.3%/yr and GDP ~1.9%/yr through 2050, a ~1.5%/yr fall in intensity — i.e., decoupling. Falling intensity does not mean falling total energy use.

Much primary energy is lost as rejected energy (mostly waste heat). LLNL's 2023 flow chart estimated U.S. energy at 93.6 quads, with 32.1 quads of energy services and 61.5 quads rejected (~34% useful).
Electricity is a lossy carrier: in EIA's 2025 data the electric power sector's output split into 13.8 quads of electricity sales (41%) and 19.7 quads of electrical system energy losses (59%).
U.S. electricity transmission and distribution losses averaged about 5% of electricity transmitted and distributed over 2018-2022.
A typical U.S. residential customer purchased about 10,791 kWh of electricity in 2022, roughly 899 kWh per month.

conflictingEvidence.issue: End-use sector shares differ depending on accounting method.
positions: Direct primary energy by sector: transportation and industry dominate; residential and commercial appear small.
Total energy by sector (electricity and electrical system losses distributed back to purchasing sectors): building sectors' shares are substantially larger.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are published by EIA and both are correct; the lesson presents the direct-use figures explicitly and explains why the building sectors look small in that view and grow in the distributed view.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Reporting year differs across EIA products at the time of research (2024 complete-year figures vs the 2025 source-and-sector chart).
positions: 2024 Today-in-Energy: ~94 quads, fossil 82%, petroleum 35.3, natural gas 34.2 (record), coal 7.9 (lowest since 1949).
2025 source-and-sector chart (dated April 2026): ~96 quads, petroleum 35.9, natural gas 34.6, coal 8.7.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson anchors on the 2025 chart (the most recent EIA source-and-sector dataset) and dates every figure to 2025; the fossil share is ~82% in both years.

rightsIssues: All sources are U.S. government (EIA) or a U.S. national laboratory (LLNL). Treated as REFERENCE_ONLY factual data; no source prose was reproduced. Figures are facts, not copyrightable expression, and were re-synthesized into original wording.
